en:
יִסּוּרָא, יְסוּ׳, יִיסּוּ׳ Chaldaic
1) (see אִיסוּרָא) chain; prison. Targum Sheni (to Esther) Esther I, 2 end לבושי יִיסּוּרֵיה his prison clothes; (Targum Jeremiah LII, 33 איסוריה).—plural יִסּוּרִין, יִיסּ׳, יִיסּוּרֵי, יְסוּ׳. Targum Eicha III, 6.—Targum Isaiah XXVIII, 22 (ed. Vilna יְסיּ׳).

—2) chastisement, suffering. Targum Jeremiah XXX, 14.—plural as ab. Ib. 11 (see אִיסוּרָא II). Targum Yonatan Vayikra XX, 5; and from—Berakhot 60ᵃ י׳ בעי וכ׳ Manuscript Munich (ed. יסורים h. form) that man desires to bring suffering upon himself. Bava Metzia 84ᵇ קביל עליה י׳ he submitted patiently to sufferings. Ib. 85ᵃ; and from Eicha Rabbah introduction end למימר לית יִיסּוּרַיָּא חשיבין וכ׳ as if saying, sufferings count to me for nothing.
comments.sourceHeRef: מילון יסטרוב, יִסּוּרָא א׳

en:
מְשִׁיכְלָא m. (שכל, Shaf. of כּוּל; compare מְכִילָא, מְכִילְתָּא)
1) a wash-basin. Shabbat 77ᵇ (phonetic etymol.) מ׳ מאשי כולא ‘washing everybody’, contradistinguished to משכילתא: משיא כלתא ‘washing brides’ (distinguished people). Kiddushin 52ᵇ, see מְשֵׁי.—plural מְשִׁיכְלֵי. Pirkei Avot Zar. 39ᵃ מ׳ חיורי white (glazed) basins. Bava Metzia 84ᵇ שיתין מ׳ דמא sixty basin-fuls of blood. Moʿed Katan 18ᵇ מ׳ דמני וכ׳ (Manuscript Munich sing.) basins filled with linen garments (for rinsing in the lake). Gittin 69ᵇ bottom of page—Fem. form (מַשְׁכִּילְתָּא) מְשִׁיכְלְתָא. Shabbat l. common gender. משיכ׳ Manuscript Munich (ed. משכיל׳), see supra. Chullin 47ᵇ משיכותא דמיא וכ׳ (correct accordingly) a basin of tepid water. Pirkei Avot Zar. 51ᵇ דסחיפא ליה מ׳ ארישיה (see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note 8) the idolatrous statuary has an inverted washbasin on its head.

—2) (compare כֶּלִי, מָאן as vessel and garment) a sort of cloak. Vayikra Rabbah section (Parashah) 23 (explained שמיכה, Judges IV, 18) רבנן … ורבנן דתמן אמרי במ׳ the rabbis here (in Palestine) say, it means with a sudra (סוּדְרָא), while the Babylonian rabbis say m’shikhla; Yalkut Judges 44; Yalkut Vayikra 585.
comments.sourceHeRef: מילון יסטרוב, מְשִׁיכְלָא א׳

en:
מוּךְ Chaldaic same
1) to decline, sink. Targum Yonatan II, Shemot XII, 42. Targum Habakkuk III, 6; and e. (see מְכִי).

—2) to become soft. Sanhedrin 95ᵃ מָכָא ליה ארעא וכ׳ the ground under him became soft.

—3) (denominative of מוךְ) to lay under, make a bed. Targum Psalms CXXXIX, 8.—Pesachim 49ᵃ בר מָךְ רבע one who lays under (his cloak) and lies down (at any place, a shiftless person). Taanit 6ᵇ; Berakhot 59ᵃ (a proverb) כד מפתח בבי … מוֹךְ שקיך וגני if it rains when the doors are opened (in the morning), lay down thy bag, ass-driver, and sleep (do not export, for provisions will be cheap); and e.—Part. מָאֵיךְ, מָיֵיךְ. Bava Metzia 84ᵇ הוו מָיְיכֵי ליה וכ׳ (Rashi: מָיְיכִין; Variant מייתי, see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note 1) they spread for him sixty mattresses. Taanit 21ᵇ bottom of page מאיך Arukh (ed. מך), see בִּיסְתַּרְקָא.—V. מָכָא.

Af. - אָמֵיךְ, אַמֵּיךְ
1) to lower. Targum Psalms CXIII, 6 מְמֵיךְ Manuscript (ed. מַמֵיךְ, מֵמִיךְ; h. text המשפילי).

—2) to make soft, crush. Ib. XLIV, 20 (h. text דִּכָּה).

—3) to lay under, make a bed. Targum Job XLI, 22 (h. text רפד).

en:
נְגַד, נְגִיד Chaldaic
1) (corresp. to h. מָשַׁךְ, נָטָה and אָרַךְ) to stretch; to draw, pull, spread. Targum Judges XVI, 30. Targum Devarim XXI, 3. Targum Jeremiah XLIII, 10.—Targum Psalms LV, 4 יִיגְּדוּן ed. Lag. (ed. Vilna יגרון; h. text ימיטו). Targum Yonatan Devarim XVII, 20. Targum Yonatan Shemot XII, 21 נגודו ידיכון וכ׳ withdraw your hands from (see מָשַׁךְ); and from—Sukkah 4ᵇ גּוּד אסיק וכ׳ stretch and raise the partitions, i.e. adopt the legal fiction that the partitions around the stand are prolonged so as to reach the ceiling (see דּוֹפָן). Shabbat 101ᵃ גוּד אחית וכ׳ stretch and bring the partitions down, i.e. adopt the fiction that the walls are prolonged so as to reach the bottom. Eruvin 4ᵇ לְגוּד, see לָבוּד. Gittin 68ᵇ נְגִידוּ מיניה מיכליה (Rashi: נְגוּדוּ) withdraw his food from him, reduce his rations. Bava Metzia 74ᵃ למידש ולמִנְגַּד to tread the grapes and to conduct the wine into the pit. Ib. 84ᵇ נַגְדוּ מתותיה וכ׳ they drew from under him sixty &c., see מְשִׂיכְלָא. Bava Batra 111ᵇ גוד לית וכ׳ draw (take me away from here), this man does not want to learn. Pesikta d'Rav Kahana Beshalach, p. 90ᵃ; Kohelet Rabbah to X, 8 גוד חמי לי lead the way, show it to me. Bekhoroth 44ᵇ נגדו ליה גלימא they spread for him (held up between him and the people) a cloak. Eruvin 94ᵃ שקולו … נְגִידוּ בה take a cloak and spread it (as a partition); and see from—Pirkei Avot I, 13 נְגַד שמא וכ׳ he who stretches his fame (is ambitious), will lose his name.

—2) to lash, see Pa.

—3) to guide, rule. Targum Ruth I, 1 (h. text שפט).

—4) to grow long; to be drawn, follow after; to flow. Targum Job XXI, 33 (h. text ימשוך). Targum Jeremiah VI, 4 (h. tex ינטו). Targum Song of Songs I, 4 נְגִדְנָא וכ׳ we are drawn after &c. Targum Devarim XXXIII, 13; 22; and from (see נְגַר).—Bava Batra 91ᵇ והוה נָגֵיד חוטא וכ׳ a line of honey flowed over both his arms; Yerushalmi Peah VII, 20ᵃ bottom of page ונ׳ מלא וכ׳ and honey flowed as much as my hands could hold; and e.—Part. pass. נְגִיד stretched, fainting (see Ithpeel). Targum Psalms LXXXVIII, 16.—Shabbat 152ᵃ, see Ithpeel

Pa. - נַגֵּד (denominative of נִגְדָּא II) to lash, punish. Targum Song of Songs VII, 5 למִינְגַּד … לנַגָּדָא.—Ketubot 33ᵇ נַגְּדוּהָ, see אִלְמָלֵא. Kiddushin 12ᵇ נַגְּדֵיה כרב punish him in accordance with Rab’s practice. Pesachim 52ᵃ ולִינַגְּדֵיה מר נַגּוּדֵי Manuscript (ed. נגידי, correct accordingly) why do you not order him to be lashed?; and e.

Af. - אַנְגִּיד to declare liable to lashes. Kiddushin l. common gender.; Yevamot 52ᵃ, and e. רב מַנְגִּיד (על) וכ׳ Rab decreed punishment for him who &c. Kiddushin l. common gender. לא מינגיד רב (read: מנגיד, as) Yevamot l. common gender.

Ithpeel - אִתְנְגִיד, אִתְנְגַד, , אִינְּגִיד, Ithpaal אִתְנַגַּד
1) to be drawn, to extend; to run. Targum Isaiah XXXIV, 11. Targum Yonatan Bamidbar XXV, 8. Targum Yonatan Breishit XLV, 19. Targum Isaiah XLIV, 3; and e.

—2) to spread, invade. Targum I Samuel XXVII, 10 (h. text פשט); and e.

—3) to be withdrawn. Targum Joshua IV, 18; and e.

—4) [to stretch one’s self,] to faint, fall away, die (h. גָּוַע). Targum Breishit XXV, 8; and from—Pesachim 50ᵃ חלש וא׳ כי וכ׳ was sick and fainted (seemed to be dead), and when he came to &c.; Bava Batra 10ᵇ. Sanhedrin 39ᵃ א׳ ואתנח he became faint and sighed; Shabbat 152ᵃ נגיד ואתנח.

—5) to be lashed. Makkot 11ᵃ; Pesachim 113ᵇ מִינְּגִיד, see זִיגּוֹד.—[Kiddushin 12ᵇ מינגיד, see supra.]
comments.sourceHeRef: מילון יסטרוב, נְגַד א׳

en: נַמְטָא f. (מוּט or מְטֵי) felt-mattress, felt-cloth. Yoma 69ᵃ; Beitzah 15ᵃ, see גְּמַד.—plural נַמְטֵי. Bava Metzia 84ᵇ, see מוּךְ Chaldaic Bava Kamma 119ᵇ מאי בגדים נ׳ what kind of garments is meant? Felt-spreadings; ib. 93ᵇ

comments.en: Some commentaries explain that although those whom he convicted were in fact wicked, Rabbi Elazar was nevertheless concerned that perhaps righteous people would have descended from them. The continuation of the story shows that the reverse was the case, as Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, was actually the cause of the birth of many righteous sons (Ma’ayanei HaĤokhma).
comments.he: יש מי שפירש שחשש ר' אלעזר שאם גם הנידונים עצמם היו רשעים, שמא היה יוצא מהם זרע צדיקים. ובאמת לפי ההמשך רואים להיפך, ר' אלעזר הוא שגרם להביא בנים צדיקים רבים לעולם (מעיני החכמה).

sections.en: After this digression, the Gemara returns to the story of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon. And although his flesh did not putrefy, even so Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, still did not rely on his own opinion, as he was worried that he may have erred in one of his decisions. He accepted afflictions upon himself as atonement for his possible sins. At night his attendants would spread out sixty felt bed coverings for him. In the morning, despite the bed coverings, they would remove sixty basins of blood and pus from underneath him.
sections.he: וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי לָא סְמַךְ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ, קַבֵּיל עֲלֵיהּ יִסּוּרֵי. בְּאוּרְתָּא הֲווֹ מָיְיכִי לֵיהּ שִׁיתִּין נַמְטֵי, לְצַפְרָא נָגְדִי מִתּוּתֵיהּ שִׁיתִּין מְשִׁיכְלֵי דְּמָא וְכִיבָא.

en: לַפְדָּא m. (לפד, compare לפת) pap, especially of figs. Shabbat 37ᵇ bottom of page (Hilkhot Rabbeinu Alfasi ליפתא). Bava Metzia 84ᵇ שתין מיני ל׳ sixty kinds of pap.—plural לַפְדֵּי. Nedarim 50ᵇ (explained כלופסין) מינא … דעבדין מנהין ל׳ a species of figs of which pap is made. Ib. אלפא מיני ל׳.

sections.en: The following day, i.e., every morning, his wife would prepare for him sixty types of relish [lifda] made from figs, and he would eat them and become healthy. His wife, concerned for his health, would not allow him to go to the study hall, so that the Rabbis would not push him beyond his limits.
sections.he: לִמְחַר עֲבַדָה לֵיהּ דְּבֵיתְהוּ שִׁיתִּין מִינֵי לַפְדָּא וְאָכֵיל לְהוּ וּבָרֵי. וְלָא הֲוָת שָׁבְקָא לֵיהּ דְּבֵיתְהוּ לְמִיפַּק לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לִדְחֲקוּהוּ רַבָּנַן.

en:
מְרַד, מְרֵיד Chaldaic
1) = h. מָרַד I, to rebel, run away. Targum I Kings XV, 27 (h. text קשר). Targum Sheni (to Esther) Kings IX, 14 (ed. Vilna מריד; h. text קשר Hithpaël). Targum Jeremiah VIII, 5 למִמְרַד מן ed. Lag. (ed. למרד) to run away from (desert); and from—Berakhot 44ᵃ עד דמריד until he ran away (bewildered).

—2) compare מֶרֶד II and רָדָה) to rule. Targum Eicha I, 7.

Ithpeel - אִימְּרִיד to become rebellious, run away. Ketubot 63ᵇ אִימְּרִידָא Rashi (ed. אִימְרְדָה, Hilkhot Rabbeinu Alfasi אִימְרְדָא) ran away (from her husband). Bava Metzia 84ᵇ אימרדה אזלה וכ׳ (Manuscript Munich אימרי׳, see מְרִי) she ran away and went to her paternal home.
comments.sourceHeRef: מילון יסטרוב, מְרַד א׳

sections.en: In the evening, he would say to his pains: My brothers and my friends, come! In the morning he would say to them: Go away, due to the dereliction of Torah study that you cause me. One day his wife heard him inviting his pains. She said to him: You are bringing the pains upon yourself. You have diminished the money of my father’s home due to the costs of treating your self-imposed afflictions. She rebelled against him and went back to her father’s home, and he was left with no one to care for him.

חֲבִילָה f. (חָבַל 2)
1) connection, whatever is in a connected state. Kelim XVIII, 9 המטה מיטמאת ח׳ וכ׳ a couch gets unclean only when combined, and can become clean again &c., opposed איברים; Sukkah 16ᵃ

—2) bundle, load, baggage, luggage. Yerushalmi Terumot X, 47ᵇ top, see זֵיר. Bava Metzia 72ᵇ המוליך ח׳ וכ׳ if one carries a load (as a messenger) from one place to another (where prices are higher). Kiddushin 65ᵇ וח׳ עמהם and have luggage with them. Bava Metzia 78ᵃ כשבאת ח׳ לידו when the working man has left a bundle (of tools) with him (as a pledge that he will come to work); and from—plural חֲבִילוֹת, חֲבִילִין, constr. (mostly) חֲבִילֵי. Shabbat XVIII, 2 ח׳ קש וכ׳ bundles of straw &c.—Yerushalmi Berakhot VII, beginning 11ᵃ מג׳ ח׳ from three different bundles (of hyssop). Bava Kamma 10ᵃ bottom of page מרבה בח׳ Manuscript Munich (ed. sing.) one adding bundles (of dry twigs) to the fire.—Berakhot 49ᵃ, and e. אין עושין מצות ח׳ ח׳ we must not perform religious duties bundle-wise (but pay attention to each singly). Eruvin 54ᵇ (reference. to Mishlei XIII, 11) אם עושה … ח׳ ח׳ מתמעטת Manuscript Oxford (see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note) if one studies bundle-wise (too many subjects at a time), his learning will decrease (ed. מתמעט he will become poorer in learning). Bava Metzia 84ᵇ הקפתנו ח׳ תשובות וכ׳ Manuscript Munich (see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note) thou hast surrounded us with bundles of arguments which contain no substance; and from

—3) band, bandage. Pirkei Avot Zar. 10ᵇ, sq. נתפרדה ח׳ the bond (of friendship between the two nations) is severed—plural חֲבִילִין. Vayikra Rabbah section (Parashah) 14; Yalkut Job 905 עשוייה … ח׳ ח׳ consists of cells, convolutions and bands (muscles).

—4) pledge, see חֲבוֹלָה.

en: מַיִם m. plural (Biblical Hebrew; compare מָהָה) water, fluid; secretion; solution. Constr. מֵי; plural מֵימוֹת, constr. מֵימֵי. Sanhedrin 108ᵃ גלגל העין שדומה למ׳ the eye-ball which (in restlessness) resembles water, see גַּלְגַּל. Parah VIII, 9 המ׳ המוכים וכ׳ smitten waters (springs or lakes formed through a catastrophe, see Sanhedrin l. common gender.). sections.en: Meanwhile, there were these sixty sailors who came and entered to visit Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon. They brought him sixty servants, each bearing sixty purses, and prepared him sixty types of relish and he ate them. When they had encountered trouble at sea, these sailors had prayed to be saved in the merit of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon. Upon returning to dry land, they presented him with these gifts.

sections.en: One day, the wife of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, said to her daughter: Go and check on your father and see what he is doing now. The daughter came to her father, who said to her: Go and tell your mother that ours is greater than theirs, i.e., my current financial status is greater than that of your father’s household. He read the verse about himself: “She is like the merchant-ships; she brings her food from afar” (Proverbs 31:14). As he was unhindered by his wife from going to the study hall, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, ate and drank and became healthy and went out to the study hall.
sections.he: יוֹמָא חַד, אֲמַרָה לַהּ לְבַרְתַּהּ: זִילִי בְּקַי בַּאֲבוּךְ מַאי קָא עָבֵיד הָאִידָּנָא? אָתְיָא, אֲמַר לַהּ: זִילִי אֱמַרִי לְאִימִּיךְ: שֶׁלָּנוּ, גָּדוֹל מִשֶּׁלָּהֶם. קָרֵי אַנַּפְשֵׁיהּ: ״הָיְתָה כׇּאֳנִיּוֹת סוֹחֵר מִמֶּרְחָק תָּבִיא לַחְמָהּ״. אֲכַל וּשְׁתִי וּבְרִי נְפַק לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא.

en:
טְהֵר, טְהַר Chaldaic same
1) to be clean (usually דכי). Berakhot 2ᵇ וט׳ גברא, see infra.

—2) to be cleared away, be gone. Ib. 2ᵃ, sq. (reference. to Vayikra XXII, 7 ובא השמש וטהר) ממאי דהאי … והאי וטהר ט׳ יומא דלמא … ט׳ גברא how do you know that this uba hash-shemesh means his sunset (the finished sunset of the seventh day, see Manuscript Munich in Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l.), and v’taher means, the day is gone; may be uba &c. means the approach of his evening (beginning sunset. Tosafot and l.; Rashi: the arrival of his (eighth) morning), and v’taher (referring to the man) means, the man becomes clean (by means of his sacrifice, Rashi).

sections.en: The students brought sixty questionable samples of blood before him for inspection, to determine whether or not they were menstrual blood. He deemed them all ritually pure, thereby permitting the women to engage in intercourse with their husbands. The Rabbis of the academy were murmuring about Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and saying: Can it enter your mind that there is not one uncertain sample among them? He must be mistaken. Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, said to them: If the halakha is in accordance with my ruling, let all the children born from these women be males. And if not, let there be one female among them. It turned out that all of the children were males, and they were called Elazar in his name.

comments.en: How could Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, instruct his wife to neglect the mitzva of burial? The commentaries suggest that the Sages considered burial a form of atonement for the deceased, which he did not need, due to his acceptance of afflictions upon himself during his lifetime (Maharsha). Others explain that Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, did not actually die at that point in time. Rather, he suffered from an illness that prevented him from enjoying the company of others. He therefore requested that his wife allow him remain in his attic, where she alone would attend to him. The Gemara relates that despite his illness, his body remained in a healthy state, as evidenced by the blood that appeared in place of a fallen hair. He would rule on halakhic questions from the attic. These rulings sounded muffled and distant, like an echo, due to his weakened state (Pardes Rimmonim).
comments.he: ושאל המהרש"א: כיצד ביטל ר' אלעזר מצות עשה של קבורה. והוא הסביר כי לדעת חכמים קבורה היא משום כפרה למת, והוא ידע בעצמו שאינו זקוק עוד לכפרה, שהרי נתמרק ונזדכך על ידי יסורים. אכן היה מי שפירש כל זה בדרך רמז, ששנים רבות היה ר' אלעזר מדוכא ביסורים ולא יכול לבוא בין הבריות מפני חוליו הגדול, ולכן ביקש שאשתו תניחנו בעליה שלא יכביד עליה ביותר, והיא היתה באה מפעם לפעם לטפל בו. וסיפר כי על אף יסוריו ומחלתו נשאר גופו ביסודו בריא, עד שכשנתלשה שערה היה יוצא ממנו דם. ומן העליה היה פוסק הלכה לבריות בקול חלוש (שנשמע כהד, כבת קול). ולכן לא ידעו בו שמת עד שנתגלה הדבר על ידי החלום (פרדס רימונים).

sections.en: As Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, was dying, he said to his wife: I know that the Rabbis are angry at me for arresting several thieves who are their relatives, and therefore they will not properly tend to my burial. When I die, lay me in my attic and do not be afraid of me, i.e., do not fear that anything will happen to my corpse. Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said: Rabbi Yonatan’s mother told me that the wife of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, told her: I laid him in the attic for no less than eighteen years and for no more than twenty-two years.
sections.he: כִּי הֲוָה קָא נָיְחָא נַפְשֵׁיהּ, אֲמַר לַהּ לִדְבֵיתְהוּ: יָדַעְנָא בִּדְרַבָּנַן דִּרְתִיחִי עֲלַי, וְלָא מִיעַסְקִי בִּי שַׁפִּיר. אַוגְנְיַן בְּעִילִּיתַאי וְלָא תִּדְחֲלִין מִינַּאי. אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי: אִישְׁתַּעְיָא לִי אִימֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן, דְּאִישְׁתַּעְיָא לַהּ דְּבֵיתְהוּ דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: לָא פָּחוֹת מִתַּמְנֵי סְרֵי, וְלָא טְפֵי מֵעֶשְׂרִין וּתְרֵין שְׁנִין אַוגְנֵיתֵיהּ בְּעִילִּיתָא.

sections.en: His wife continued: When I would go up to the attic I would check his hair, and when a hair would fall out from his head, blood would come and appear in its place, i.e., his corpse did not decompose. One day I saw a worm emerging from his ear, and I became very distressed that perhaps his corpse had begun to decompose. My husband appeared to me in a dream and said to me: It is no matter for concern. Rather, this is a consequence for a sin of mine, as one day I heard a Torah scholar being insulted and I did not protest as I should have. Therefore, I received this punishment in my ear, measure for measure.

כּוֹל, כּוֹלָא, כּוֹלָּא Chaldaic = h. כֹּל
1) all, every one; any. Constr. כָּל (frequ. used absolutely). Targum Onkelos Breishit XVI, 12, sq. Targum Shemot XX, 9. Targum Yonatan Devarim XXXII, 49 לא כל היאך not at all as (thou sayest); and from—Yerushalmi Yoma VIII, 45ᵇ bottom of page לא כולא מן הדין וכ׳ all does not depend upon this man (it is not at all within his power) to say to the king, Thou art no king, i.e. his saying that the Day of Atonement has no atoning power, cannot affect its power; Yerushalmi Shevuot II, 33ᵇ bottom of page—Sanhedrin 46ᵇ, and from (לאו) לא כל כמיניה all is not as if dependent on him, i.e. he has no power to &c. Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 79, beginning (explained בכלח, Job V, 26) תבא בכולא אלי וכ׳ (some ed. בכוֹלָּה) thou shalt enter the grave in fulness, full, wanting nothing.—כָּל דְּכֵן = h. כָּל שֶׁכֵּן, see כֹּל. Targum Job IV, 19; and from—Niddah 51ᵃ; and from—כָּל עלמא, see infra.—With suffix כּוּלָךְ, כּוּלֵיה &c. (Buxt. כֻּלָּךְ &c.) all of thee, of him &c., entire. Targum Breishit XXV, 25; and from—Yoma 14ᵇ כוליה יומא the entire day; ib. 19ᵃ (not כולי). Ib. 26ᵃ כּוּלְהוּ מצפרא אתו (see Rabbinowicz Diḳduḳé Sof’rim (Variæ Lectiones &c., Munich 1867-84) and l. note 10) all of them come in (for their share) by the lots cast in the morning; and from—plural constr. כּוּלֵי all of. Targum Esther VI, 1 כ׳ ליליא (ed. Lag. כוליה). Targum Kohelet X, 12 כ׳ עלמא (ed. Lag. כוליה).—Yerushalmi Berakhot II, 4ᵇ כ׳ עלמא ידעין ed. Lehm. (ed. כל) all the world, all people know (abbr. כ"ע); Yerushalmi Moʿed Katan III, 83ᶜ bottom of page כל עמא; see עָלְמָא. Kiddushin 79ᵇ, see כּוּל Chaldaic—כ׳ האי all of that, to that extent. sections.en: During this period, when two people would come for adjudication of a dispute, they would stand by the doorway to the home of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon. One litigant would state his side of the matter, and the other litigant would state his side of the matter. A voice would issue forth from his attic, saying: So-and-so, you are guilty; so-and-so, you are innocent. The Gemara relates: One day, the wife of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, was quarreling with a neighbor. The neighbor said to her as a curse: This woman should be like her husband, who was not buried. When word spread that Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, had not been buried, the Rabbis said: This much, i.e., now that the matter is known, to continue in this state is certainly not proper conduct, and they decided to bury him.
sections.he: כִּי הֲווֹ אָתוּ בֵּי תְרֵי לְדִינָא, הֲווֹ קָיְימִי אַבָּבָא, אָמַר מָר מִילְּתֵיהּ וּמַר מִילְּתֵיהּ נָפֵיק קָלָא מֵעִילִּיתֵיהּ, וְאָמַר: אִישׁ פְּלוֹנִי אַתָּה חַיָּיב, אִישׁ פְּלוֹנִי אַתָּה זַכַּאי. יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא מִינַּצְיָא דְּבֵיתְהוּ בַּהֲדֵי שִׁבָבְתָּא, אֲמַרָה לַהּ: תְּהֵא כְּבַעֲלַהּ שֶׁלֹּא נִיתַּן לִקְבוּרָה. אָמְרִי רַבָּנַן: כּוּלֵּי הַאי וַדַּאי לָאו אוֹרַח אַרְעָא.

פְּרִידָה f. (פָּרַד)
1) one of a pair of pigeons, single pigeon, opposed to קֵן. Kinn. III, 6 צריכה … פ׳ אחת she is bound to offer a single pigeon in addition; Zevachim 67ᵇ. Sifra Vayikra, N’dab., Chaldaic VIII, Parah 7; Zevachim 65ᵃ אפי׳ פ׳ אחת וכ׳ he may offer even one single pigeon; and from—plural פְּרִידִין (m.), פְּרִידוֹת. Kinn. l. common gender. דין … Bavli ed. (Mishnah ed. דות …). Sifra l. common gender.; and from—Transferred a dear person. Bava Metzia 84ᵇ פ׳ אחת יש לי … ואי אתם וכ׳ one pigeon (my son’s body) is among you, and you will not let him come to me (be buried by my side)? Ib. פ׳ … ואתם וכ׳ I have a dear son among you, and you want to deprive me of him (expose him to the evil eye by showing him too much honor)?—plural פְּרִידוֹת. Bava Kamma 38ᵇ שתי פ׳ טובות וכ׳ two fine pigeons (precious proselytes) do I expect to bring forth from among you (see בָּרַךְ Hifil).

—2) a single berry; a slice of a pomegranate. Yerushalmi Berakhot VI, 10ᵃ top פ׳ אחת של ענב one grape berry; פ׳ אחת של רמון one slice of a pomegranate. Yerushalmi Nazir VI, 54ᵈ [read:] פ׳ של רמון … שחלקה בפיו ואכלה a piece of a pomegranate of ʿOrlah (see עָרְלָה) which one cut off with his mouth and ate. Yerushalmi Ma'asrot I, 48ᵈ; and e.

—3) pebble, particle. Niddah 27ᵃ, sq. על פ׳ אחת של רקב to one particle of decayed matter; על פ׳ אחת של עפר to one particle of earth. Yerushalmi Yoma II, 39ᶜ top ברוב כל פ׳ ופ׳ (the fire must have seized) the larger portion of every particle, opposed רובו של קומץ the larger portion of the handful (of the meal offering); and e.—plural פְּרִידוֹת. Niddah l. common gender.—[פרידה Chaldaic, see פְּרִידָא I.]

sections.en: There are those who say that the Sages found out that Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, had not been buried when Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, his father, appeared to them in a dream and said to them: I have a single fledgling among you, i.e., my son, and you do not wish to bring it to me by burying him next to me. Consequently, the Sages went to tend to his burial. The residents of Akhbaria, the town where the corpse of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, was resting, did not allow them to do so, as they realized that all the years that Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, had been resting in his attic, no wild beast had entered their town. The townspeople attributed this phenomenon to his merit and they did not want to lose this protection.
sections.he: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי אִיתְחֲזַאי לְהוּ בְּחֶלְמָא, אֲמַר לְהוּ: פְּרֵידָה אַחַת יֵשׁ לִי בֵּינֵיכֶם, וְאִי אַתֶּם רוֹצִים לַהֲבִיאָהּ אֶצְלִי? אֲזוּל רַבָּנַן לְאִעֲסוֹקֵי בֵּיהּ, לָא שְׁבַקוּ בְּנֵי עַכְבְּרַיָּא, דְּכֹל שְׁנֵי דַּהֲוָה נָיֵים רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בְּעִילִּיתֵיהּ לָא סְלִיק חַיָּה רָעָה לְמָתַיְיהוּ.

1) watering station, especially in Palestine for Temple pilgrims.—plural בֵּירָאוֹת, בֵּירָייוֹת, בֵּירָיוֹת. Eruvin II, 1; and from Yerushalmi ib. 20ᵇ top לביריי׳ ולא לבירות (read לבירייות ולא לבורות) for watering stations but not for cisterns; see Bavli ib. 18ᵃ

Beiträge zur Sprach- und Alterthumsforschung, by Michael Sachs, Berlin 1852—54, 2 vols, see Berliner (editor of Targum Onkelos) a. Hildesh z. Geogr. p. 21).—b) B. or Be-B. in Babylon, native place of Ulla, R. Dostai, and oth. Pirkei Avot Zar. 40ᵃ. Eruvin 56ᵃ מולייתא דבי ב׳ וכ׳ the ascents between Berai and Narash. Sotah 10ᵃ בי בארי. Eruvin 45ᵃ בירי. [Chullin 127ᵃ ביברי דנרש, read בי בירי ונרש.]

comments.en: Allegorically, the serpent is the cause of death and impurity in the world, as its advice led to the sin of Adam and Eve. For most people death can be a fearful experience. One who has perfected and refined himself during his lifetime has no need to fear death. Rather than being a negative and fearful experience, for such an individual death is actually spiritually elevating. In this context, the serpent, i.e., death, is portrayed as protecting Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Elazar’s father, symbolizing his righteousness (see Ritva and Tosafot).

sections.en: One day, which was Yom Kippur eve, everyone in the town was preoccupied with preparations for the Festival. The Rabbis sent a message to the residents of the adjacent town of Biri instructing them to help remove the body of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, from the attic, and they removed his bier and brought it to his father’s burial cave. They found a serpent [le’akhna] that had placed its tail in its mouth and completely encircled the entrance to the cave, denying them access. They said to it: Serpent, serpent! Open your mouth to allow a son to enter next to his father. It opened its mouth for them and uncoiled, and they buried Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, alongside his father.

en: חוֹל III (Biblical Hebrew; חלל) [outside of the sanctuary, foreign,] profane, common, opposed קוֹדֶשׁ; week-day, opposed שַׁבָּת, מוֹעֵד. Pesachim 104ᵃ; Chullin 26ᵇ בין קודש לח׳ between what is sacred and what is secular. Shevuot 35ᵇ כל שמות … חוץ מזה שהוא ח׳ all names of lordship (Adonay) … are sacred, except the following which is secular (referring to persons).—חוֹלוֹ של מועד, or חול המועד the half-festive days intervening between the first and the last days of Passover or of Succoth. Megillah 22ᵇ; and from—Ma'aser Sheni III, 8 פתוחות לח׳ having an entrance on secular ground; ib. תוכן ח׳ their inside is secular ground. Bava Metzia 84ᵇ כלי … ישתמש בו ח׳ shall the vessel once used for sacred things, be used for secular purposes (shall R. Eleazar’s widow marry Rabbi)?; and see from—plural חוּלִּין profane things, animals &c. not consecrated, ordinary objects. Chullin 2ᵇ, and e. ח׳ שנעשו על וכ׳ ordinary food (not T’rumah) prepared with the precautions required for the levitical cleanness of consecrated food.—Pesachim 22ᵃ, and from ח׳ שנשחטו בעזרה animals not consecrated for sacrifices which were slaughtered in the Temple court. Ib., and from ח׳ … דאורייתא the law forbidding the use of ordinary animals slaughtered &c., is not Biblical. Gittin 62ᵃ עיסת חוּלָּיו his ordinary dough; זיתי חוליו (not ים …), see טָהֳרָה. Chagigah I, 3 באות מן הח׳ are procured from secular funds, opposed to proceeds from second tithes; and from—Berakhot 32ᵃ (play on ויחל, Shemot XXXII, 11) ח׳ הוא לך וכ׳ it is too foreign to thy nature to do such a thing; Yalkut Breishit 83, see חָלִילָה.—Ḥullin (= שְׁחִיטַת ח׳), name of a treatise of the Mishnah, Tosefta and Talmud Babli, of the Order of Kodashim, containing the laws concerning ordinary meat.

sections.en: The Gemara continues: After this incident, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent a messenger to speak with the wife of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and propose marriage. She sent a message to him in response: Shall a vessel used by someone sacred, i.e., Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, be used by someone who is, relative to him, profane? There, in Eretz Yisrael, they say that she used the colloquial adage: In the location where the master of the house hangs his sword, shall the contemptible shepherd hang his basket [kultei]? Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent a message back to her: Granted that in Torah he was greater than I, but was he greater than I in pious deeds? She sent a message back to him: Whether he was greater than you in Torah I do not know; but I do know that he was greater than you in pious deeds, as he accepted afflictions upon himself.

sections.en: The Gemara asks: With regard to Torah knowledge, what is the event that demonstrated the superiority of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, over Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi? The Gemara answers: When Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa, the leading Sages of the generation, were sitting on benches [asafselei] teaching Torah along with the other Sages, the youthful pair Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would sit before them on the ground out of respect.

sections.en: These two young students would engage in discussions with the Sages, in which they would raise difficulties and answer them brilliantly. Seeing the young scholars’ brilliance, the leading Sages said: From their waters we drink, i.e., we are learning from them, and they are the ones sitting on the ground? Benches were prepared for Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and they were promoted to sit alongside the other Sages.

פְּרִידָה f. (פָּרַד)
1) one of a pair of pigeons, single pigeon, opposed to קֵן. Kinn. III, 6 צריכה … פ׳ אחת she is bound to offer a single pigeon in addition; Zevachim 67ᵇ. Sifra Vayikra, N’dab., Chaldaic VIII, Parah 7; Zevachim 65ᵃ אפי׳ פ׳ אחת וכ׳ he may offer even one single pigeon; and from—plural פְּרִידִין (m.), פְּרִידוֹת. Kinn. l. common gender. דין … Bavli ed. (Mishnah ed. דות …). Sifra l. common gender.; and from—Transferred a dear person. Bava Metzia 84ᵇ פ׳ אחת יש לי … ואי אתם וכ׳ one pigeon (my son’s body) is among you, and you will not let him come to me (be buried by my side)? Ib. פ׳ … ואתם וכ׳ I have a dear son among you, and you want to deprive me of him (expose him to the evil eye by showing him too much honor)?—plural פְּרִידוֹת. Bava Kamma 38ᵇ שתי פ׳ טובות וכ׳ two fine pigeons (precious proselytes) do I expect to bring forth from among you (see בָּרַךְ Hifil).

—2) a single berry; a slice of a pomegranate. Yerushalmi Berakhot VI, 10ᵃ top פ׳ אחת של ענב one grape berry; פ׳ אחת של רמון one slice of a pomegranate. —3) pebble, particle. Niddah 27ᵃ, sq. על פ׳ אחת של רקב to one particle of decayed matter; על פ׳ אחת של עפר to one particle of earth. Yerushalmi Yoma II, 39ᶜ top ברוב כל פ׳ ופ׳ (the fire must have seized) the larger portion of every particle, opposed רובו של קומץ the larger portion of the handful (of the meal offering); and e.—plural פְּרִידוֹת. Niddah l. common gender.—[פרידה Chaldaic, see פְּרִידָא I.]

sections.en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said to the other Sages present: I have a single fledgling among you, i.e., my son Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and you are seeking to take it from me? By promoting my son to such a prestigious position at such a young age, his chances of being adversely affected by the evil eye are greatly increased. They demoted Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to sit on the ground, at his father’s request. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa said to the Sages: Should one who has a father to care for him, i.e., Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, be demoted so that he may live, while the other one, who does not have a father to care for him, i.e., Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, should be allowed to die? Upon hearing his argument, the Sages also demoted Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, without explaining to him the reason for his demotion. He became offended and said to them: You are equating Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to me, by demoting us together. In fact, I am much greater than he.
sections.he: אָמַר לָהֶן רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: פְּרֵידָה אַחַת יֵשׁ לִי בֵּינֵיכֶם, וְאַתֶּם מְבַקְּשִׁים לְאַבְּדָהּ הֵימֶנִי? אֲחֲתוּהּ לְרַבִּי. אָמַר לָהֶן רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה: מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אָב יִחְיֶה, וּמִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ אָב יָמוּת? אֲחֲתוּהּ נָמֵי לְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן. חֲלַשׁ דַּעְתֵּיהּ, אָמַר: קָא חָשְׁבִיתוּ לֵיהּ כְּווֹתִי?

sections.en: As a result of that incident, the relationship of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi changed. Up until that day, when Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would state a matter of Torah, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, would support him by citing proofs for his opinion. From this point forward, when they were discussing a subject and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would say: I have an argument to respond, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, would preempt him by saying to him: Such and such is what you have to respond, and this is the refutation of your claim. Now that you asked these questions, you have surrounded us with bundles of refutations that have no substance, i.e., you have forced us to give unnecessary answers. Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, would anticipate Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s comments and immediately dismiss them as having no value.
sections.he: עַד הָהוּא יוֹמָא כִּי הֲוָה אָמַר רַבִּי מִילְּתָא הֲוָה מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: מִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ כִּי הֲוָה אָמַר רַבִּי ״יֵשׁ לִי לְהָשִׁיב״, אָמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: כָּךְ וְכָךְ יֵשׁ לְךָ לְהָשִׁיב, זוֹ הִיא תְּשׁוּבָתְךָ. הַשְׁתָּא הִיקַּפְתָּנוּ תְּשׁוּבוֹת חֲבִילוֹת שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶן מַמָּשׁ.

רָעַע (Biblical Hebrew) [to bring in close contact, see רֵיעַ,]
1) to strike against, shatter, impair. —Part. pass. רָעוּעַ; f. רְעוּעָה; plural רְעוּעִים, רְעוּעִין; רְעוּעוֹת impaired, defective; in a ruinous state, threatening, opposed בריא sound. Kiddushin 39ᵇ סולם ר׳ a broken ladder. Kelim III, 5 הר׳ a cracked vessel. Taanit 20ᵇ מפולת שאמרו בריאות ולא ר׳ the falling of houses which they mention (ib. III, 4) means the falling of sound buildings, but not of such as were out of repair; and from

—2) (neut. verb) רַע, imperf. יֵרַע to be injurious, evil; רע ל־ to grieve, displease. Bava Metzia 84ᵇ בני אל ירע לך my son, let it not grieve thee; and e.

Piël - רֵעַע to shatter, break.—Part. pass. מְרוֹעָע; f. מְרוֹעַעַת; plural מְרוֹעָעִים, מְרוֹעָעִין; מְרוֹעָעוֹת. Kohelet Rabbah to III, 2 השרוי בבית המר׳ he who dwells in a threatening house; Yerushalmi Shabbat II, 5ᵇ top מְרוֹעֲרַע (from רִעְרֵעַ). Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 32 קנקנים מר׳, see קַנְקָן I. Yerushalmi Taanit III, 66ᵈ top מְרוֹעֲרָעִים threatening buildings; and from

Hithpaël - הִתְרָעֵעַ,

Nithpaël - נִתְרָעֵעַ, , Hithpol. הִתְרוֹעֵעַ, Nithpol. נִתְרוֹעֵעַ to be shaken, cracked, become defective. Menachot 53ᵇ (reference. to Jeremiah XI, 16) מקול מיליהן … נִיתְרָעֲעוּ דליותיהן וכ׳ from the sound of the words of the spies were the branches (young men) of Israel broken; Yalkut Jeremiah 289 נרתעו (read: נִתְרָעוּ). Sotah 48ᵃ (play on ערה, Zephaniah II, 14) אפי׳ בית … מִתְרוֹעֵעַ even a house which lies in a thicket of cedars will be shaken; Yalkut Isaiah 292 מתנועע (correct accordingly). Yerushalmi Sanhedrin X, 27ᵈ bottom of page לכיפה … כיון שנִתְרוֹעֲעָה אחת מהן נִתְרוֹעֲעוּ כולן like a heap of stones, when one of them is shaken (disturbed), all of them are shaken; Yerushalmi Moʿed Katan III, 83ᶜ שנִתְרַעְרְעָה … נִתְרַעְרְעוּ (from רערע); Breishit Rabbah section (Parashah) 100 וכולה מִתְרוֹעַעַת; and e.

Hifil - הֵרַע
1) to shake, impair. Yerushalmi Sheviit X, 39ᵈ top מֵירַע כוחן it impairs their prerogatives; ib. מוֹרַע (from יָרַע). Yerushalmi Pesachim VII, 34ᵈ top שהוֹרַעְתָּ כחו וכ׳ whose standing thou declarest impaired in the case of an ascertained uncleanness. Shemot Rabbah section (Parashah) 8 הֵרֵעוּ לנפשם they did harm to themselves; and e.—V. הֲרָעָה.

—2) to be evil; ה׳ ל־ to displease. Midrash Tanḥuma Sh’laḥ 5; Bamidabar Rabbah section (Parashah) 167 וה׳ לאביו and it displeased his father; and e.—[
3) to join, combine, see רָעָהPiël]

comments.en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi thought that the expertise of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, in Torah was a result of his greater effort, and that upset him. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s father therefore explained to him that one’s erudition is not solely a result of his toil. In this case, Rabbi Shimon was such a brilliant scholar that his son, Rabbi Elazar, had inherited great intellectual acumen (Ma’ayanei HaĤokhma).

sections.en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi became offended. He came and told his father what had transpired. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said to him: My son, do not let his actions offend you, as he is a lion, son of a lion, and you are a lion, son of a fox. Rabbi Elazar’s father, Rabbi Shimon, was a renowned Sage, and therefore Rabbi Elazar’s sagacity is not surprising. In any event, this incident demonstrates the superiority of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi with regard to knowledge of Torah.
